Schools assign summer projects for students with the goal of continuing education during break periods to prevent learning loss over extended time away from the classroom. There is merit to both teacher designed and student designed summer projects, but on balance, allowing students to design their own projects is preferable.

Student designed projects empower students to take ownership of their own learning. When students have autonomy in choosing a topic they find genuinely interesting to research or a skill they want to develop, they are more motivated to dedicate time and effort into completing a high quality project. Intrinsic motivation drives deeper learning compared to completing assignments solely to satisfy a teacher's requirements. By letting students follow their own interests and curiosity, student designed projects can inspire a lifelong love of learning. 

However, teacher designed projects provide structure to ensure students cover topics from the curriculum and meet learning benchmarks. Without teacher guidance, some students may choose projects that do not align with educational standards or fail to provide sufficient educational benefit. Teacher designed projects also allow for assessment against predetermined rubrics, facilitating grading and feedback. 

An ideal solution balances these perspectives. Teachers could provide parameters and topics related to the curriculum but allow flexibility for students to put their own creative spin on the project. For example, a science teacher may request a project on the human body and give examples of options like creating a model, research paper or documentary film. Within that guideline, students can further define the specific focus and format based on their personal interests. This gives direction while still empowering student voice and choice.

Overall, the benefits of cultivating student independence, motivation and leadership in their own education outweigh purely teacher directed learning outside the classroom. By granting more freedom to design their own meaningful summer projects, schools can further engage and inspire students to be active participants in their lifelong academic journey.

The electoral college is a system used to select the President of the United States in which citizens vote for a slate of electors who then cast their votes for a candidate. The system has been in place since the United States Constitution was adopted in 1787, but there is ongoing debate about whether it works effectively. The purpose of this essay is to explore the arguments for and against the electoral college system.

Those who defend the electoral college argue that it ensures that the President is elected by the entire country rather than just by the population of a few large cities. This is because the electoral college is made up of electors who are typically appointed by state political parties and who are elected by the states, not by individual citizens. This means that each state's electors have an equal say in the election, regardless of the population of that state. Additionally, the electoral college allows for a candidate to run for President without having to win every single state, which would be unrealistic.

Another argument in favor of the electoral college is that it provides a moderating influence on the election process. Because states in different regions of the country can have significantly different political views, the electoral college can help to balance out the influence of the large cities on the election. This helps to ensure that the President is elected based on the will of the country as a whole, rather than just on the basis of a few cities.

However, opponents of the electoral college argue that it is not fair to the American people. They argue that the electoral college system undermines the principle of "one person, one vote," because citizens in large states have more influence over the election than citizens in smaller states. This is because each state's electors are awarded based on the population of that state, so states with larger populations have more electoral votes than states with smaller populations. This means that the voices of citizens in smaller states are silenced, and is why some states are even known as "safe states" where one party wins automatically.

Another argument against the electoral college is that it is outdated and no longer reflective of the modern political reality. With the rise of campaign spending and the influence of big money over politics, small states are no longer able to compete with big states in terms of the resources available to campaign in their state. As a result, the influence of states with smaller populations is even further diminished, making it harder to hold the elected President accountable to the entire country. Additionally, the electoral college system does not reflect the cultural diversity of the United States. Because states are divided into certain regions, the electoral college does not help to bring together the diverse groups of people that make up the United States.

In conclusion, the electoral college system has its advantages and disadvantages. While it ensures that the President is elected by the entire country rather than just by the population of a few large cities, it is also fair to say that the system is not fair to the American people. The electoral college undermines the principle of "one person, one vote," and is also outdated and no longer reflective of the modern political reality.

The Challenge of Exploring Venus

The allure of space exploration has always been a captivating topic for humanity. Among the many celestial bodies, Venus, Earth's closest neighbor, presents a unique set of challenges and opportunities for exploration. This article delves into the complexities and potential rewards of venturing into this hostile yet intriguing world.

Exploring Venus has always been a daunting task due to its harsh environment. The planet's temperature exceeds 800 degrees Fahrenheit and its atmosphere is dense with carbon dioxide. The immense atmospheric pressure, nearly 90 times that of Earth, makes land-based missions extremely difficult. Past attempts have seen spacecraft succumb to these conditions within hours of landing.

Despite the challenges, recent technological innovations provide hope for the exploration of Venus. For example, floating research stations that are situated above the perilous surface conditions are being developed. Such innovations allow for extended study of Venus from a relatively safe distance, without having to contend with the hostile surface environment. However, these ideas are in their early stages, and their feasibility remains to be tested under real conditions.

While orbiting or hovering missions can provide valuable information about the planet, they have limitations. The dense atmosphere of Venus impairs the capacity of these missions to gather comprehensive data about the planet's surface. This limitation underscores the need for more direct exploration methods, albeit with significant technological advancements.

Venus offers several compelling reasons for exploration. It shares several geological features with Earth and was once more Earth-like than it is today. Understanding Venus's evolution could provide crucial insights into planetary science, including Earth’s own future. Additionally, Venus's proximity to Earth during certain orbits makes it a relatively accessible destination for planetary exploration.

The potential scientific gains of exploring Venus are substantial, but there are risks involved. The hostile environment coupled with current technological limitations presents significant hurdles. Therefore, it is crucial to develop robust, innovative technologies capable of withstanding Venus's harsh conditions.

In conclusion, the exploration of Venus is a challenging but worthwhile pursuit. While it comes with risks and challenges, the potential scientific gains are substantial. The development of robust, innovative technologies capable of withstanding Venus's harsh conditions is crucial for the success of such missions. As space exploration continues to advance, Venus remains a testament to the enduring human spirit of discovery, beckoning us to unravel its mysteries despite the dangers that lie ahead.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to express my strong support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote.

The Electoral College is a system that was devised in the 18th century and is no longer fit for purpose in the 21st century. Under the Electoral College, each state is allocated a certain number of electors, based on the number of representatives it has in the House of Representatives plus its two senators. The candidate who wins the popular vote in a state wins all of that state's electoral votes, except Maine and Nebraska, which award their electoral votes proportionally.

This system is deeply unfair. It means that a candidate can win the popular vote but lose the election, as happened in 2000 and 2016. It also means that candidates have no incentive to campaign in states that are already decided, as they know that they will not win any electoral votes there. This results in a two-tiered system, in which some states are effectively ignored by the candidates.

The Electoral College also gives an unfair advantage to small states. A voter in Wyoming has three times the voting power of a voter in California, simply because Wyoming has three electoral votes and California has 55. This is because each state has a minimum of three electoral votes, regardless of population.

The Electoral College is also undemocratic. It is a system in which a few people, the electors, can decide the outcome of the election, even if the majority of voters have voted for a different candidate. This is simply not acceptable in a democracy.

I urge you to support abolishing the Electoral College and electing the president by popular vote. It is the only way to ensure that all voters are equal and that the president is elected by the will of the people.

Thank you for your time.

In a competitive world where automobiles keep getting faster, drivers are more reckless, and the death toll is rising, a solution to maintain public safety is necessary. Distracted and careless drivers may no longer be a public menace with the rise of a new technology, driverless cars. Driverless cars are beneficial to the public because the cars will have a better sense of the world around them, and they will eliminate most of the dangers of drunk and/or drowsy drivers.

The continued evolution of a self driving car has created many advanced sensors that can sense and adjust to the world around it more efficiently than any human.

According to "Driverless Cars Are Coming," a sensing system called LIDAR that "uses laser beams to form a constantly updating 3D model of the car's surroundings." This would eliminate the current problem of blind spots and reduce the rate of collisions dramatically. The LIDAR system would also be able to instantly sense any changes in the surrounding area, whereas a human would only be aware of a change if he/she looked in the correct mirror, or when a collision was already happening. There has also been an advance in wheel sensors. According to "Driverless Cars Are Coming", these sensors can detect various dangerous situations and can "...cause the car to apply brakes on individual wheels and reduce power from the engine, allowing far better response and control than a human driver could manage alone." Obviously, these sensors can keep the passengers and public safer than just one unassisted driver.

Along with more advanced features, comes the elimination of many public menaces and dangerous drivers. If a driver is drowsy, they won't be endangering the public, because the car would be driving for them. There won't be any slip of the wheel to send a car into a ditch, a heavy foot accelerating the car into a tree or pedestrian, or fender benders because the driver was unable to apply the brake. Of course, if the car would happen to need a driver, the safety sensors could easily wake up the sleeping passenger with vibrating seats, as mentioned in paragraph seven of "Driverless Cars Are Coming," voices demanding the driver to take over, and other alarms to wake the driver up. In the case of drunk driving, even though they may need to take the wheel in certain situations, it would be quite rarely, and would still decrease the danger of drunk drivers. Someday the self driving car may no longer need any human assistance, which would eliminate the danger of drowsy and drunk drivers all together.

In conclusion, the creation of self driving cars would be beneficial to overall public safety because the developing sensors can already detect and adapt to changes more efficiently than a human can, and it would eliminate the danger of sleeping, distracted, and drunk drivers.

In the recent years, the concept of driverless cars has rapidly gained popularity. Autonomous vehicles are vehicles that can operate without the need for a human driver, using technologies such as artificial intelligence and advanced sensors. Driverless cars have the potential to bring about a significant transformation in the transportation industry, offering numerous benefits to society while simultaneously raising some concerns.

One of the most significant benefits of driverless cars is the potential to increase road safety. Human error is a leading cause of accidents on the road, and driverless cars have the potential to eliminate this risk entirely. Autonomous vehicles are equipped with advanced sensors and machine learning algorithms that allow them to detect obstacles, other vehicles, pedestrians, and other hazards on the road. This enables them to make split-second decisions and react to changing road conditions, reducing the likelihood of accidents.

Another significant advantage of driverless cars is the potential to reduce traffic congestion. Autonomous vehicles can communicate with each other and coordinate their movements, allowing them to avoid traffic jams and reduce the overall flow of traffic on the road. This can help to reduce the amount of time drivers spend stuck in traffic, which can have a significant impact on their productivity and quality of life.

Driverless cars also have the potential to increase accessibility for people with disabilities. Autonomous vehicles can be equipped with features that make them more accessible for people with mobility impairments, such as ramps, lifts, and automated driving systems. This can help to improve the mobility and independence of people with disabilities, providing them with greater opportunities to participate in society and live fulfilling lives.

However, while there are many benefits to driverless cars, there are also some concerns that need to be addressed. One of the biggest concerns is the potential for job losses in the transportation industry. As driverless cars become more widespread, there may be a significant reduction in demand for drivers, which could lead to widespread unemployment in the transportation sector.

Another concern is the cost of driverless cars. Autonomous vehicles are currently very expensive, with some high-end models costing hundreds of thousands of dollars. This could make it difficult for many people to afford them, which could limit their availability to the wider public.

Finally, there are concerns about the safety of driverless cars. While autonomous vehicles have the potential to be incredibly safe, there is still the risk of malfunctions or errors in the technology. These could have serious consequences for the drivers and passengers of the vehicle, so it is important that safety measures are put in place to mitigate these risks.

In conclusion, driverless cars have the potential to bring about a significant transformation in the transportation industry. They offer numerous benefits, including increased road safety, reduced traffic congestion, and increased accessibility for people with disabilities. However, there are also some concerns that need to be addressed, including job losses, cost, and safety concerns. As the technology continues to develop, it is important that these concerns are addressed to ensure that driverless cars are safe, accessible, and affordable for all.

Title: A Cowboy Who Rode the Waves

Have you ever heard the story of a cowboy who rode waves? It might seem like an unlikely tale, but believe it or not, there really was such a person – a man named Pancho Pirelli.
Pancho Pirelli was a true cowboy, raised on a ranch in the rugged landscape of the American West. His love for the wild, open plains and his skill with a lasso led him to become a champion rodeo rider.
However, his life took an unexpected turn when he discovered surfing during a trip to Hawaii. The powerful waves of the Pacific Ocean captivated him, and he couldn't resist trying it out.
At first, Pancho struggled to adapt to the new sport. The surfboard felt strange under his feet, and it took a lot of patience to master the art of riding the waves. But with his determination and cowboy spirit, he quickly improved and fell in love with surfing.
As Pancho continued to surf and hone his skills, he began competing in surfing competitions. His cowboy roots helped him stand out from the crowd, and soon people began calling him the "Cowboy of the Waves."
Pancho's unique blend of cowboy charm and surfing prowess attracted fans from both worlds. He became famous not only for his impressive riding style but also for his warm personality and genuine love of the water.
The Cowboy of the Waves continued surfing and competing for many years, until one day he decided to return to his beloved ranch in the American West. He left behind the ocean waves but took with him the spirit and passion he gained from riding them. His story serves as an inspiration to those who might feel limited by their backgrounds, reminding us that it is never too late to discover new passions and pursue our dreams, regardless of our past experiences.

In a competitive world where automobiles keep getting faster, drivers are more reckless, and the death toll is rising, a solution to maintain public safety is necessary. Distracted and careless drivers may no longer be a public menace with the rise of a new technology, driverless cars. Driverless cars are beneficial to the public because the cars will have a better sense of the world around them, and they will eliminate most of the dangers of drunk and/or drowsy drivers.

The continued evolution of a self-driving car has created many advanced sensors that can sense and adjust to the world around it more efficiently than any human.

According to "Driverless Cars Are Coming," a sensing system called LIDAR that "uses laser beams to form a constantly updating 3-D model of the car's surroundings." This would eliminate the current problem of blindspots and reduce the rate of collisions dramatically. The LIDAR system would also be able to instantly sense any changes in the surrounding area, where as a human would only be aware of a change if he/she looked in the correct mirror, or when a collision was already happening. There has also been an advance in wheel sensors. According to "Driverless Cars Are Coming", these sensors can detect various dangerous situations and can "...cause the car to apply brakes on individual wheels and reduce power from the engine, allowing far better response and control than a human driver could manage alone." Obviously, these sensors can keep the passengers and general public safer than just one unassisted driver.

Along with more advanced features, comes the elimination of many public menaces and dangerous drivers. If a driver is drowsy, they won't be endangering the public, because the car would be driving for them. There won't be any slip of the wheel to send a car into a ditch, a heavy foot excelerating the car into a tree or pedestrian, or fender benders because the driver was unable to apply the brake. Of course, if the car would happen to need a driver, the safety sensors could easily wake up the sleeping passenger with vibrating seats, as mentioned in paragraph seven of "Driverless Cars Are Coming," voices demanding the driver to take over, and other alarms to wake the driver up. In the case of drunk driving, even though they may need to take the wheel in certain situations, it would be quite rarely, and would still decrease the danger of drunk drivers. Someday the self-driving car may no longer need any human assistance, which would eliminate the danger of drowsy and drunk drivers all together.

In conclusion, the creation of self-driving cars would be beneficial to overall public safety because the developing sensors can already detect and adapt to changes more efficiently than a human can, and it would eliminate the danger of sleeping, distracted, and drunk drivers.

Urban sprawl is a problem that has become increasingly common in recent decades. In cities around the world, populations are growing at an exponential rate, resulting in the development of urban areas ever further out from the city center. This process of rapid outward growth – known as urban sprawl – can have serious consequences for both people and their environment. The most obvious consequence of urban sprawl is increased traffic congestion on roads leading into and out of major cities. As more homes move further away from city centers, more vehicles are required to transport residents to work or school each day. This often results in gridlock during rush hour periods, making commutes longer and less pleasant than before. This particular identification sparked a series of debates, theories, and unconventional interpretations. The Face on Mars phenomenon gained momentum as a result of its unusual resemblance, captivating the public's interest and generating theories about ancient Martians, their possible extinction, and the existence of a lost civilization existing on the Red Planet.

Research on exoplanets, extraterrestrial environments, and their potential to sustain higher forms of life have drawn from the experience and lessons learned about Mars.



In conclusion, The Face on Mars remains a topic of profound controversy and interest. Its unusual appearance and lack of definitive scientific explanations have been the subject of extensive debate and interpretations. The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a way to analyze and categorize human facial expressions. It was developed by Dr. Paul Ekman and Dr. Wallace Friesen in the 1970s. FACS is based on the idea that there are a limited number of basic facial movements that can be combined to create a wide variety of emotions. By understanding these basic movements, it becomes possible to recognize and interpret facial expressions accurately.
The FACS system consists of 43 different action units, each describing a specific facial movement. These action units are further organized into 14 distinct facial action categories. These categories are:
1. Inner brow raiser
2. Outer brow raiser
3. Eyelid raiser
4. Upper lid raiser
5. Lower lid raiser
6. Eyebrow lowerer
7. Nose wrinkler (nasalis)
8. Cheek raiser
9. Lip corner depressor
10. Lip presser
11. Lip corner puller
12. Lip corner puller and lip presser
13. Lips part
14. Mouth stretch

The FACS system has proven to be a valuable tool for various fields, such as psychology, law enforcement, and animation. It allows experts to analyze and categorize facial expressions accurately, which can be used to detect deceit or understand human emotions. In the world of animation, FACS is utilized by animators to create believable and expressive characters.
In conclusion, the FACS system is an essential tool for studying and categorizing human facial expressions, providing a comprehensive understanding of the basic movements that make up our emotions.

I am writing as a citizen and voter of our great state to discuss an issue that I believe is central to our democracy: the method in which we elect the President of the United States. I am aware of the ongoing discussions regarding either keeping the Electoral College or moving to choosing our president by popular vote. After careful consideration and examination of numerous perspectives and sources, I argue in favor of preserving the Electoral College system.

Although the Electoral College has been criticized—for lack of direct democracy, for the focus on swing states, and for the potential discrepancy with the national popular vote—it serves pertinent roles in our electoral process. As noted in the article "In Defense of the Electoral College" by Judge Richard A. Poster, the Electoral College provides five compelling reasons for its maintenance. Escape from a national dispute over the popular vote allows for a guaranteed and certain outcome (18). It propels a presidential candidate to appeal beyond regional boundaries, fostering a sense of belonging among voters across the nation (19). It gives crucial attention to the swing states, encouraging the voters of these states to be more engaged and thoughtful in their electoral decision (20). Furthermore, it tips the balance back towards larger states, which lose some of their influence due to the equal representation in the Senate (21). Additionally, it prevents the nation from the complication and burden of runoff elections, even when the popular vote remains inconclusive (22).

The views presented in the article "The Indefensible Electoral College" by Bradford Plume also deserve due consideration. Plume argues that the Electoral College can lead to confusions and potential mishaps like 'disaster scenarios' and faithless electors acting against voters' will (11). However, as Poster points out, such incidents have been rare (16) and the trust in electors has generally been upheld within the Electoral College system (15).

The Electoral College system also galvanizes the voters who do exercise their right despite their awareness that their single vote would unlikely tip the national scales, a testimony to their willingness to express political preference rather than indifference or disenchantment (23). Therefore, we must invest more in raising awareness about the workings of the Electoral College and more importantly, in fostering an environment that encourages participation in this great democratic exercise. 

In conclusion, while the Electoral College presents certain challenges, I believe the robust nature of this system has proven its value over the past centuries and made necessary adaptations to the changing times. What this means is that the popular vote within a state wins the electoral votes of the electors who then vote for the president. Many people dislike this system including myself. I disprove of this system because it limits representation, permits the disinterest of voters, and reduces a candidates interest in a state.

One major problem with the Electoral College voting system is that it limits representation of the people. The Electoral College votes work so that the population of a state directly effects the amount of votes that states receives. For example, Wyoming only has about 500,000 voters so it only receives one electoral college vote. Because there is only one vote for Wyoming, the 500,000 voters do not have accurate representation in a vote that has a total of 270 electoral votes. There have also been times in which a president has won the popular vote but lost the Electoral College vote. This was seen in the 2000 vote of Bush versus Gore when Gore won the popular vote and Bush won the electoral vote.

One might claim that because the amount of electoral votes for a state is based of the population, it is fair. However, I believe that the popular vote is more fair because it expresses the opinion of the majority. In some states, there is a large majority of people running for a single party. This can be observed primarily in Texas where an overwhelming majority of voters are Republican. Therefore, the Republican president wins Texas almost every election period. This can be frustrating for Democrats who live in Texas because they know that their vote does not matter causing them to lose interest in voting in the first place. This is not fair for those people nor is it particularly good to express as an American trait.

As stated before, the larger the population of a state, the more Electoral College votes that state gets. This leads to a small group of "big states" that have such a large amount of votes, they are the target for candidates to try to persuade to vote for them. On the opposite side of the spectrum, most of the other 50 states have a smaller amount of votes and are less of an objective for candidates to acquire. In many states throughout an election period (the period in which candidates move to different states giving speeches) the candidates never make an appearance in their state at all. This is observed in the 2000 election in which seventeen states did not have the candidate make an appearance at all. This also can lower interest in voting for the president.

The Electoral college voting system is not fair in the way the present system works. The system does not show proper representation of the people, does not promote interest in voting, and causes a candidate to ignore the states in which do not have a large amount of electoral votes. Moving to popular vote will fix all of these problems and will improve the way we vote for our president.

Unfortunately, despite the importance of socialization, we have not yet learned how to raise children who can help bring about a better society. There are several reasons for this. One is that there is a lack of consensus on what constitutes "healthy" socialization. Different cultures, regions, and even families have different ideas about what values and behaviors are desirable, which can make it difficult to establish a universal standard for socialization. Additionally, there is a lack of effective guidance on how to achieve positive socialization outcomes. Parents, educators, and other caregivers may not have the knowledge, skills, or resources to provide children with the type of socialization they need to thrive.

Another reason why we have not yet learned how to raise children who can help bring about a better society is that there are many factors that can interfere with the socialization process. For example, poverty, violence, and discrimination can all have a negative impact on children's development, making it harder for them to learn positive socialization skills. Additionally, technology and social media have changed the way children interact with each other and with the world around them, creating new challenges and opportunities for socialization.

Despite these challenges, there are still many examples of effective socialization practices. For instance, research has shown that children who grow up in families that emphasize communication, empathy, and cooperation tend to be more successful in school, work, and relationships. Similarly, schools that promote positive socialization, such as by encouraging teamwork and community service, have been shown to improve academic outcomes and reduce problematic behaviors. There are also many community based programs, such as mentoring and after school programs, that aim to provide children with positive socialization experiences.

One promising approach to improving socialization outcomes is to address the root causes of negative socialization. For example, addressing poverty and inequality can help to reduce the stress and trauma that can interfere with children's development. Promoting social and emotional learning in schools can help to teach children the skills they need to succeed in relationships and in life. Encouraging positive values, such as empathy and respect, can help to create a culture of kindness and cooperation.

In conclusion, the destiny of society is inextricably linked to the socialization of its children. While we have not yet learned how to raise children who can help bring about a better society, there are many promising approaches that can help to promote positive outcomes. By working together to address the root causes of negative socialization and promoting positive values and behaviors, we can help to ensure that future generations are equipped to thrive in a rapidly changing world.

Sharks are often feared as dangerous predators of the sea, but these amazing creatures play a crucial role in maintaining healthy ocean ecosystems. Sharks have been swimming our oceans for over 400 million years and yet their populations have rapidly declined due to human activities such as accidental killing during fishing, hunting for fins and meat, habitat destruction from coastal development, bycatch from trawling operations along with pollution and climate change. The consequences of shark loss range from basic ecosystem disruption to devastating economic impacts on our fisheries-based economies. Sharks are apex predators that occupy a prominent place near the top of marine food webs; they feed predominantly on medium-sized fishes and bony fish species like snappers and groupers which can accumulate high levels of toxins in their bodies. When sharks become depleted or removed entirely, entire trophic level shifts occur resulting in an increase of mid-trophic species like jacks that reduce biodiversity and alter community structure - this is known as ‘trophic cascade’. These cascades can lead to declines in prey species at lower trophic levels leading to starvation among herbivorous fish like parrotfish which help maintain natural coral reef balance by consuming seaweed that would otherwise outcompete corals for space; without them coral reefs would disappear within 40 years according to research conducted at James Cook University in Australia . . In addition to preserving ecological health, sharks also support commercial fisheries through "top down" control (organisms controlling those below them), allowing smaller fish numbers to reach higher sizes before being harvested so seafood catches may be larger; when more large predatory fish exist there is greater competition amongst themselves reducing the size of their own prey resulting fewer small fishes available for catching – conventional wisdom found around Australian Fisherman holds true “No tiger no fly” meaning if you don't see big tiger sharks then there won't be much baitfish around either!
